fp.fragment: functions are first-class values; closures and tables of methods
fp.why: Host embedding wants callbacks without a class system.
fp.useWhen: When composition and tables beat a class hierarchy.

sources.quote: All values in Lua are first-class values. This means that all values can be stored in variables, passed as arguments to other functions, and returned as results.
first-class functions allow the employment of many techniques from functional programming

oop.reason: No built-in classes; tables plus metatables emulate prototypes. Not class-OOP as the language model.

sources.quote: Every value in Lua can have a metatable. This metatable is an ordinary Lua table that defines the behavior of the original value under certain events.
Although Lua does not have a built-in concept of classes, object-oriented programming can be emulated using functions and tables.

decl.reason: Imperative procedural core with optional data-description tables.

sources.quote: Lua combines simple procedural syntax with powerful data description constructs based on associative arrays and extensible semantics.
Multi-paradigm: scripting, imperative (procedural, prototype-based, object-oriented), functional, meta, reflective

actor.reason: Coroutines are cooperative threads of execution, not actor mailboxes.

sources.quote: The type thread represents independent threads of execution and it is used to implement coroutines (see §2.6).
Lua implements a small set of advanced features such as first-class functions, garbage collection, closures, proper tail calls, coercion

static.fragment: dynamically typed: variables have no types; values do
static.why: Embeddable scripting without a compile-time checker.
static.price: Errors at the call that used the wrong value.

sources.quote: Lua is a dynamically typed language. This means that variables do not have types; only values do. There are no type definitions in the language.
As a dynamically typed language intended for use as an extension language or scripting language, Lua is compact enough to fit on a variety of host platforms.

strong.fragment: strong-dynamic with explicit number/string coercion rules; values carry types
strong.why: Eight basic types; mixed ops follow the manual, not C-style UB.
strong.useWhen: Prefer explicit conversions except documented coercions.

sources.quote: There are eight basic types in Lua: nil, boolean, number, string, function, userdata, thread, and table.
coercion(automatic conversion between string and number values at run time)

hm.reason: No static inference; values carry runtime tags.

sources.quote: There are no type definitions in the language. All values carry their own type.
As a dynamically typed language intended for use as an extension language or scripting language
There are no type definitions in the language.
It supports only a small number of atomic data structures such as Boolean values, numbers

gen.reason: No parametric generics; tables are heterogeneous.

sources.quote: Tables can be heterogeneous; that is, they can contain values of all types (except nil).
They are associative arrays with addition of automatic numeric key and special syntax.

malloc.reason: Automatic GC heap; userdata memory is host/C, not a Lua malloc API for tables.

sources.quote: Lua performs automatic memory management. This means that you do not have to worry about allocating memory for new objects or freeing it when the objects are no longer needed.
The closure is managed by Lua's garbage collector, just like any other object.

gc.fragment: automatic GC; incremental mark-and-sweep and a generational mode
gc.why: Embeddable VMs cannot ask scripts to free tables.
gc.price: Finalizers and mode switches; you tune collectgarbage.

sources.quote: Lua manages memory automatically by running a garbage collector to collect all dead objects.
Lua implements a small set of advanced features such as first-class functions, garbage collection, closures

trace.price: Step size can degenerate to stop-the-world.

sources.quote: In incremental mode, each GC cycle performs a mark-and-sweep collection in small steps interleaved with the program's execution.
In most cases it's better to replace the (usually single) link with a new table and let the GC do its work.

rc.reason: Tracing GC, not reference counting as the heap.

sources.quote: The garbage collector (GC) in Lua can work in two modes: incremental and generational.
The closure is managed by Lua's garbage collector, just like any other object.

own.reason: Tables/functions are referenced, not uniquely owned.

sources.quote: Tables, functions, threads, and (full) userdata values are objects: variables do not actually contain these values, only references to them.
Tables are the most important data structures (and, by design, the only built-in composite data type) in Lua

thr.reason: Lua threads are coroutines, not OS threads.

sources.quote: Lua threads are not related to operating-system threads. Lua supports coroutines on all systems, even those that do not support threads natively.
coroutines(cooperative multitasking)

coro.fragment: language coroutines via the thread type; yield/resume
coro.why: Cooperative multitasking inside one OS thread.
coro.useWhen: Generators, game loops, host callbacks that must yield.
coro.price: Not preemptive; one stall blocks that lua_State.

sources.quote: The type thread represents independent threads of execution and it is used to implement coroutines (see §2.6).
The LuaJIT VM is fully resumable. This means you can yield from a coroutine even across contexts, where this would not possible with the standard Lua 5.1 VM

csp.reason: No CSP channels in the language.

sources.quote: Lua threads are not related to operating-system threads.
coroutines(cooperative multitasking)

loop.reason: No language event loop; hosts (games, nginx) provide one.

sources.quote: Lua is dynamically typed, runs by interpreting bytecode with a register-based virtual machine
As a dynamically typed language intended for use as an extension language or scripting language
